findings.claim: Every practice question in all seven lessons is typed "40 marks — Shakespeare Essay" (42 questions).
findings.truth: A Christmas Carol is the 19th-century prose set text in the modern and literary heritage component. Shakespeare sits in the other component. The mark total of 40 is right; the label is not. Changed to "40 marks — 19th-century prose essay".
findings.evidence: specs/ocr/english-literature-J352.md 3a: component 01 Section B 19th century prose, 40 marks; Shakespeare is Section B of component 02.

findings.claim: Lesson 1 mark ladders read "Band 6: ... / Lower bands: less detailed." Lessons 2-7 use a four-tier ladder (Mastering / Secure / Developing / Emerging).
findings.truth: There is no Band 6 in a 40-mark question, and the four-tier names are not the house ladder. All 42 ladders rescaled to five equal house bands with mark ranges out of 40 (Top 33-40, Upper-mid 25-32, Mid 17-24, Lower-mid 9-16, Low 1-8). Lesson 1's telegraphic ladders were rewritten; lessons 2-7 keep their descriptors verbatim under the new band names plus a Low band line.
findings.evidence: Orchestrator instruction: ladders must match the real mark total (40) and use the five house bands.

findings.claim: Flashcard: "Which Parliamentary report inspired the novella?" -> "The 1843 report on child labour conditions."
findings.truth: The report is the Second Report of the Children's Employment Commission, published in 1842; Dickens read it in early 1843. Lesson 7 states this correctly, so the unit contradicted itself.
findings.evidence: L7 content_html n7: "1843, the year after the Second Report of the Children's Employment Commission".

findings.claim: "Are there no prisons? And the Union workhouses?" quoted as one continuous speech (content_html, flashcard 9, practice question 4).
findings.truth: Two separate speeches with the gentleman's reply between them. Ellipsis added.
findings.evidence: Gutenberg lines 354-358: '"Are there no prisons?" asked Scrooge. "Plenty of prisons," said the gentleman... "And the Union workhouses?" demanded Scrooge.'

findings.claim: "The clerk works in a tiny 'dismal little cell' with one shovelful of coal" (also flashcard 8).
findings.truth: Bob gets no shovelful. His fire "looked like one coal" and he cannot replenish it, because Scrooge keeps the coal-box and threatens to sack him whenever he comes in with the shovel.
findings.evidence: Gutenberg lines 179-186: 'the clerk's fire was so very much smaller that it looked like one coal. But he couldn't replenish it, for Scrooge kept the coal-box in his own room'.

findings.claim: "By ending Stave 1 with Scrooge falling into a 'heavy sleep'..."
findings.truth: Stave One ends "went straight to bed, without undressing, and fell asleep upon the instant". The "heavy sleep" is the last line of Stave Two.
findings.evidence: Gutenberg lines 1009-1010 (end of Stave I) and line 1811 (end of Stave II).

findings.claim: "the reader, unlike Scrooge, already knows the first Spirit will come at one o'clock".
findings.truth: Marley tells Scrooge the hour to his face, so Scrooge knows it too.
findings.evidence: Gutenberg line 941: '"Expect the first to-morrow, when the bell tolls One."'

findings.claim: Mark scheme for question 2 says "tracks supernatural structure across the four Spirits" while the same ladder and the lesson say three.
findings.truth: Marley is a ghost, not one of the Three Spirits. Changed to "across Marley and the three Spirits".
findings.evidence: Gutenberg line 906 onwards: '"You will be haunted... by Three Spirits."'

findings.claim: "The Ghost's 'mild' reminder, 'He has, I think, a child', lands like a soft accusation." Repeated as flashcard 8.
findings.truth: Fabricated line. The Ghost says Fan "died a woman, and had, as I think, children"; Scrooge answers "One child"; the Ghost replies "True... Your nephew!" Nothing in the passage is called mild.
findings.evidence: Gutenberg lines 1405-1411.

findings.claim: Revision tip asks for "the three main memories"; the key fact beside it lists four scenes.
findings.truth: Internal contradiction. Tip changed to four scenes to match the key fact.
findings.evidence: Same key-fact block in L3 content_html.

findings.claim: Printed extract runs Belle's speech into "A golden one" as one continuous quotation.
findings.truth: "A golden one" is Belle's answer to Scrooge's question "What Idol has displaced you?" The intervening line is now printed.
findings.evidence: Gutenberg Stave II, Belle's parting speech.

findings.claim: Tiny Tim "says, at church: 'I hope the people saw me in the church, because I was a cripple...'"
findings.truth: Tim never speaks these words. Bob reports them in the third person at the dinner table: "He told me, coming home, that he hoped the people saw him in the church, because he was a cripple..." A student quoting the first-person version would be quoting words that are not in the novella.
findings.evidence: Gutenberg lines 2184-2190.

findings.claim: "The goose is 'eked out' with 'sage and onion'".
findings.truth: "Eked out by apple-sauce and mashed potatoes, it was a sufficient dinner". Sage and onion is the stuffing, not what the goose is eked out with.
findings.evidence: Gutenberg lines 2230 and 2235.

findings.claim: Ghost of Christmas Present quoted as "a jolly Giant, glorious to see... in a simple green robe" (also flashcard 2).
findings.truth: The text reads "clothed in one simple green robe". The quoted words were not verbatim.
findings.evidence: Gutenberg lines 1885 and 1901-1902.

findings.claim: "The laundress boasts: 'He frightened every one away from him when he was alive, to profit us when he was dead!'" Repeated as flashcard 5 and in the question 2 mark scheme.
findings.truth: The charwoman says it. She is the first of the three to arrive and the one who sells the bed-curtains, the blankets and the shirt. The laundress is Mrs Dilber, who brings sheets, towels, teaspoons, sugar-tongs and boots.
findings.evidence: Gutenberg lines 3028-3030 (the three name themselves) and 3170-3174 ("laughed the same woman", i.e. the charwoman).

findings.claim: The thieves sell "his very shirt", presented as a quotation.
findings.truth: Not a quotation from the novella. The charwoman says she took the shirt off the corpse because putting it on him to be buried in was "wasting of it". Rewritten as plain description.
findings.evidence: Gutenberg lines 3144-3158.

findings.claim: Flashcard answer "'Bob broke down all at once.'"
findings.truth: The text reads "He broke down all at once."
findings.evidence: Gutenberg line 3380.

findings.claim: "Dickens gives him patience ('Bob trembled, and got a little nearer to the ruler')".
findings.truth: That line is from Stave 5 and shows the opposite of patience: Bob edges towards the ruler because he "had a momentary idea of knocking Scrooge down with it". Replaced with a real patience detail from Stave 1, where Bob tries to warm himself "at the candle".
findings.evidence: Gutenberg lines 3840-3843; line 186 for the candle.

findings.claim: Printed extract: "Tiny Tim, who bore a little crutch, and had his limbs supported by an iron frame!"
findings.truth: The text reads "Alas for Tiny Tim, he bore a little crutch, and had his limbs supported by an iron frame!"
findings.evidence: Gutenberg line 2161.

findings.claim: Flashcard answer "'Bob broke down all at once.'" (same misquote as F17).
findings.truth: The text reads "He broke down all at once."
findings.evidence: Gutenberg line 3380.

findings.claim: Question 4 prints "Read the following extract from Stave 5" above "I will honour Christmas in my heart, and try to keep it all the year. I will live in the Past, the Present, and the Future."
findings.truth: Scrooge says this at the graveside in Stave 4, before he wakes. Stave 5 begins after it.
findings.evidence: Gutenberg line 3540; Stave V starts at line 3555.

findings.claim: Flashcard: "Which Stave 5 quotation states that Scrooge's change is complete?" -> "I am not the man I was."
findings.truth: That line is Stave 4, spoken at the grave while Scrooge is still pleading with the Spirit. The card taught the wrong stave for a quotation students will use under timed conditions.
findings.evidence: Gutenberg line 3527.

findings.claim: "OCR gives you an extract plus a question asking you to start with the extract and then explore the whole novella. The command is clear: you must do both."
findings.truth: The 19th-century prose question is one extended response from a choice of two: an extract-based question making links to the whole text, OR a discursive question. The extract is not compulsory, and a student who revises only the extract drill is unprepared for half the choice.
findings.evidence: specs/ocr/english-literature-J352.md 3a: "Learners respond to one extended response-style question on their studied text, from a choice of two: An extract-based question, making links to the whole text OR A discursive question."

findings.claim: The exam-technique lesson's planning, structure and final-checks advice never mentions that accurate writing is credited on this question.
findings.truth: AO4 is assessed in Section B of each component, so spelling, punctuation, grammar and vocabulary carry marks on the novel question. Nothing in the unit denies this; it is an omission, not a false claim, so it is left unedited. Worth one line in the final checks if the orchestrator wants it added.
findings.evidence: specs/ocr/english-literature-J352.md 3h: learners are assessed on vocabulary, sentence structures and accurate spelling and punctuation (AO4) in Section B of each examined component.

summary: Seven lessons, 24 findings, 109 edits. The unit's worst faults are a fabricated Ghost line in L3, a misattributed boast in L5 (charwoman, not laundress), two Stave 4 quotations taught as Stave 5 in L7, an invented first-person Tiny Tim quotation in L4, and every one of the 42 practice questions labelled a Shakespeare essay. All quotations were checked against the Gutenberg text; no per-AO mark splits were present anywhere in the unit.
